posts.title: White Label WordPress Development: The Agency Guide
posts.excerpt: White-label WordPress development for agencies: what to send at the brief, how to check the code, what handover includes and how cost compares with hiring.
posts.content_html:
White-label WordPress development means another team builds the site and your agency delivers it as its own work. You keep the client and the margin. The partner hands everything back under your brand and never appears in front of your client.

This guide covers the brief, the code checks, the handover, the contract and the cost against hiring.

What white-label WordPress development covers

A white-label partner takes the work from an approved design to a site ready to launch. That usually means a custom theme or a child theme of one you already use. Clients who edit in Gutenberg get a block theme.

Most builds also include some of these:

  • ACF field groups and custom post types, planned before anyone builds a template.
  • Custom Gutenberg blocks or custom Elementor widgets that keep the client's edits inside the design.
  • Online shops, where WooCommerce development covers checkout, shipping and tax rules.
  • A small custom plugin where several plugins overlap to do one job.

You stay in charge of the client, the strategy, the pricing and every conversation. The partner handles production. When the partner needs an answer from the client, they ask you, and you pass it on in your own words.

What to hand over at the brief

Send whatever you have, and say what is still missing. A partner can only fix a price against what it can see, so gaps in the brief turn into scope changes later.

When a brief arrives, we check it against this list:

  • The Figma file. Mark which frames the client has approved, and include mobile frames for each template. Shared colour and text styles save hours, because we set them up once as global styles.
  • The content. Real copy and images if the client has them. If not, say who writes them and by when, because placeholder text hides layout problems until launch week.
  • The current site. Its URL and the pages that must survive, so every changed URL gets a tested redirect.
  • Hosting access. The host's name, SFTP or SSH access and somewhere to run staging. Share logins through a password-manager vault, never by email.
  • Plugins and licences. Which premium plugins the client already pays for, and whose account holds each licence.
  • Who edits what. Which people on the client's team will update the site, and how much layout freedom they need.
  • The date you have promised. The timeline in the scope works back from it.

Client names can wait until both sides have signed the NDA. Before we build, we check the host's PHP version, memory limit, caching layer and email delivery. Those limits decide what the site can safely do.

We reply to a brief within one business day and send a written scope with a fixed price within two. Our team works from Dhaka, so you can brief us at 5pm London and review progress at 9am.

How to check the quality of the code

Judge a partner's code against the rules WordPress sets for its own. The WordPress Coding Standards cover PHP, HTML, CSS, JavaScript and accessibility. The handbook says they help avoid common coding errors, make code easier to read and make later changes simpler.

You do not need to read every line yourself. Ask the partner to show you these checks on the first project:

CheckHow to test itWhat a pass looks like
Coding standardsRun PHP_CodeSniffer with the WordPress Coding Standards rulesets on the theme and custom pluginsNo errors, and a written reason for any rule switched off
Output escapingSearch the templates for variables printed to the pageEach one passes through a function such as esc_html(), esc_attr() or esc_url()
AccessibilityUse the site with a keyboard only, then spot-check with a screen readerEvery menu, form and button works, with a visible focus style
Editor experienceLog in with the role the client will use and change a pageThe content changes and the layout stays intact
PluginsAsk for the plugin listEach plugin has a stated job and a named licence holder
SpeedMeasure Core Web Vitals on a real phoneResults recorded before handover, beyond a lab score
Brand tracesRead the theme's style.css header, the plugin headers and the admin footerYour agency's name, or nobody's

Escaping deserves a closer look, because it stops injected code reaching the page. WordPress's security guidance says to escape output as late as possible, ideally as the data is printed. Code that escapes early, or not at all, is a warning sign.

For accessibility, WordPress expects its own code to meet WCAG 2.2 at level AA. That is a sensible bar for client themes too, and you can write it into the scope.

On our builds, a named producer runs the project in a shared Slack Connect or WhatsApp channel. You first see the work on a password-protected, noindexed staging site under your brand, after it has passed our published QA checklist.

What a clean handover includes

A good handover leaves nothing that depends on the partner. The client's team should be able to run the site on their own. A new developer should be able to pick it up without learning who built it.

Ask for all of this at launch:

  • The Git repository, transferred to your account or the client's.
  • An editing guide in your brand that shows the client which parts they can change.
  • A list of every plugin with its licence holder.
  • Hosting, domain and plugin accounts held in your name or the client's, never the partner's.
  • The partner's access revoked, with the removal confirmed in writing.
  • Staging taken down. We remove ours within 14 days of launch unless you ask us to keep it.

Settle user roles before launch too. We set up the client's team so they can publish and edit, while plugin installs and theme settings stay with an administrator.

Handover does not have to end the work. Before SoftVolt AI, our founder built Heat Pumps 4 Pools, a WooCommerce store for a UK pool-heating retailer. His maintenance engineering on the store carried on after launch.

That is the same care-plan pattern agencies resell under their own brand. On our builds, if something inside the agreed scope breaks after launch, we fix it at our cost.

How a partner protects your client relationship

Protection belongs in the contract, where you can enforce it. Before you share a client's name, ask any partner to put these in writing:

  • A mutual NDA, on their template or yours, signed before the brief.
  • A promise not to approach, market to, quote for or accept work from your client, during the project or after it.
  • No footer credit, watermark or "built by" line. Commit messages, staging domains and documents should carry your brand.
  • Credentials kept in a shared vault, with least-privilege access instead of owner logins.
  • A data processing agreement wherever client personal data is involved.

We sign all of these. Our team works from Dhaka, and Bangladesh is not on the EU adequacy list. For UK and EU client data, we work under the UK IDTA or Addendum, EU Standard Contractual Clauses and an Article 28 agreement.

One practical test helps. Ask what the partner does if your client contacts them directly. A good answer sends everything back through you.

Our security and confidentiality page lists every practice we follow, from encrypted devices to staging sites that stay private.

Cost: a white-label partner or an in-house hire

A hire costs more than the salary. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the median annual wage for web developers at $92,650 (May 2025, read in October 2026). Benefits, payroll taxes, equipment and your management time come on top.

In the UK, employers pay Class 1 National Insurance at 15% on earnings above £5,000 a year in 2026 to 2027. On an illustrative £40,000 salary, that adds £5,250 a year before pension contributions, a laptop or any time spent managing the work.

A white-label partner swaps that fixed cost for a price per project or a monthly plan. Ours work like this:

  • Essential, from £500 a month: 1 active project and up to 5 pages per project. It covers WordPress and WooCommerce builds in 10 to 15 business days.
  • Growth, from £1,200 a month: up to 3 active projects and 10 pages per project. It adds headless Next.js, with a turnaround of 7 to 10 business days.
  • Premium, from £2,400 a month: up to 6 active projects and 15 pages per project. It adds AI automation, SEO and paid media, in 5 to 7 business days.
  • Enterprise, quoted: unlimited active projects, with turnaround agreed in writing.

Work outside a plan gets its own written scope and fixed price. Hosting and premium plugin licences are billed at cost or held in your account, with no mark-up.

Hire when you have full-time WordPress work every month and someone to manage it. Use a partner when the volume rises and falls. A partner also fits briefs that need skills one hire will not have, such as a headless front end.

Send us your WordPress brief

If you have a WordPress project with a date attached, send the brief as it stands. Our white-label WordPress development service page explains how we build. The written scope comes back with a fixed price within two business days.

Send the brief or book a call. Ask for the NDA first if you want it signed before you name the client.

posts.title: How to Choose a White Label Web Development Partner
posts.excerpt: Choosing a white label web development partner? Ask these 12 questions before you sign, from NDAs and code ownership to defect fixes and exit terms.
posts.content_html:
To choose a white label web development partner, ask twelve questions before you sign. Judge every answer with one test: is it specific, and will they put it in the contract? Vague answers on confidentiality, code ownership or bug fixes turn into arguments later, often in front of your client.

Below are the questions we would ask in your place and what a good answer sounds like. Each one ends with how SoftVolt AI answers it, taken from our own published terms.

12 questions to ask a white label web development partner

Ask them on a call, then ask for the answers in writing. A partner who answers well on the phone but will not write it down has given you a sales answer.

1. Will you sign a mutual NDA before I share the client's name?

You will share client names, plans and sometimes customer data before any contract exists. So the NDA has to come first, not with the proposal.

A good answer: "Yes, a mutual NDA, on our template or yours, before you send the brief." Be wary of a one-way NDA that only protects the partner, or a request to see the brief first.

Our answer: We sign a mutual NDA, on our template or yours, before you share a client's name. Ask for it in your first message and it arrives before we discuss anything else.

2. Will you ever contact my client?

A good answer: "Never, and the contract says so, including after the project ends." The clause should cover marketing to your client, quoting for them and taking work from them directly. Ask about portfolio use and credit links too, because both can reveal you.

Our answer: We will not approach, market to, quote for or accept work from your client, during the project or after it. We add no footer links, watermarks or "built by" credits. If your client asks a technical question, we write the answer for your account manager to send.

3. Who owns the code, and when does it pass to us?

Paying for code does not automatically make it yours. The UK Intellectual Property Office says a contractor usually keeps the copyright in their work unless a contract says otherwise. See the IPO guidance on who owns copyright.

US law lists nine kinds of commissioned work that can count as "work made for hire", and software is not one of them. The Copyright Office explains this in Circular 30 on works made for hire. Either way, you want ownership settled in writing.

A good answer: "The contract assigns the code to you or your client, and we move the repository into your account at handover." Ask your solicitor to read the clause, because this article is not legal advice.

Our answer: Your agency or your client owns the code, whichever you decide. We transfer the repository and all credentials at handover. Theme and plugin headers name your agency, not us.

4. What does your QA cover, and can I read the checklist?

A good answer: a written checklist they use on every build, covering browsers, real devices, accessibility and page speed. They should also check each page against the approved design. "We test everything" with no document behind it is not an answer.

Our answer: Every build passes our published QA checklist before you see it: cross-browser, real-device, accessibility and Core Web Vitals checks. We compare each page with your Figma frames before it reaches you.

5. When are you online, and how does that match my day?

A good answer: working hours in your time zone, the hours of overlap and the name of the person who replies during them. A partner in another time zone can work in your favour when you plan the hand-offs.

Our answer: The team works from Dhaka (UTC+6, no daylight saving) and covers 09:00 to 23:00 local time. Dhaka afternoons overlap the UK working day, evenings overlap East Coast mornings in the US and Canada, and mornings overlap the Sydney afternoon.

Brief us at 5pm London and review the work at 9am. A named producer answers in your shared Slack Connect or WhatsApp channel.

6. How do you price work, and what changes the price?

A good answer: a fixed price against a written scope, or a monthly plan with clear limits, plus a written process for changes. Open-ended hourly billing moves the risk onto you. Ask whether they add a margin to hosting, plugins and licences.

Our answer: You get a written scope and a fixed price within two business days of the brief. Nothing starts until you approve it.

If your client asks for something new, we write the change down with a price before anyone builds it. We bill hosting, plugins and licences at cost, or you hold them in your own accounts.

7. How many of our projects can you run at once?

A good answer: a number. "As many as you need" means nobody has planned for your busy month. Ask what happens to briefs above that number and how they handle a rush.

Our answer: Essential (from £500 a month) runs 1 active project at a time. Growth (from £1,200) runs up to 3, Premium (from £2,400) up to 6, and Enterprise has no limit and a custom quote. You can queue as many briefs as you like, and our rates page lists what each plan includes.

For rush work, we tell you the cost if we can hit the date. If we cannot, we say so instead of taking the work and missing it.

8. Can I see work you have built?

A good answer: live sites you can open yourself, with the partner's role stated honestly. A good white label partner cannot show agency work without permission, so a short portfolio is fine. A portfolio full of other agencies' client sites should make you ask whether yours will join it.

Our answer: Partner work only appears with the agency's written permission, and then under the agency's brand. Instead we show live builds our founder delivered before SoftVolt AI, such as the Heat Pumps 4 Pools WooCommerce store.

Our founder, Md Alamgir Hossen, has nine years of PHP, WordPress, WooCommerce and Elementor work for agencies in the UK and Bangladesh. Most recently he led the WordPress team at a UK agency.

9. Where will my client's logins and data live?

A good answer: a shared password vault, the lowest access level the work needs, two-factor authentication and access removed at the end. For personal data from UK or EU clients, add a data processing agreement and a lawful transfer route.

If the partner works outside the UK and EU, ask which transfer route they use. The ICO explains the UK IDTA and Addendum for international transfers. The European Commission lists the countries with an EU adequacy decision.

Our answer: Credentials live in a shared 1Password or Bitwarden vault, never in email or chat. We ask for a scoped role, such as a limited WordPress role, instead of the owner's login. Every workstation is disk-encrypted and every account we hold uses two-factor authentication.

Bangladesh is not on the EU adequacy list. So we sign an Article 28 data processing agreement and work under the UK IDTA or Addendum and EU Standard Contractual Clauses. Our security and confidentiality page lists every practice.

10. What do we get at handover?

A good answer: a list, not a promise. Expect the repository, credentials, documentation and an editing guide your client can follow. You should also get every plugin with its licence holder, plus written confirmation that the partner's access is gone.

Our answer: You get the repository, a handover document, an editing guide in your brand and a plugin list with licence holders. We remove our access and confirm it in writing. We keep staging sites password-protected and noindexed, and remove them within 14 days of launch unless you ask us to keep them.

11. Who pays when something breaks after launch?

A good answer: the partner fixes defects in the agreed scope at its own cost. Ask how they tell a defect from a new request, and how long the cover lasts.

Our answer: If it was in the agreed scope and it breaks, we fix it at our cost, with no invoice. New requests get a written price first. For updates, backups and monitoring, our maintenance plans run under your brand, and you can resell them as your own care plan.

12. How do we end it if it does not work?

A good answer: monthly or project-by-project terms, no exclusivity, and a clean handover whatever the reason. The promise not to contact your client should outlast the contract.

Our answer: Plans run month to month with no long-term contract, and you can move up or down as your workload changes. We ask for no exclusivity and no minimum spend. A project ends when you sign the handover, and our promise not to approach your client continues after we stop working together.

A scorecard to take into the call

Tick each row as you go. If two or more answers land in the right-hand column, keep looking.

TopicListen forWalk away if
NDAMutual, signed before the briefThey want the brief first
Client contactNever, in writing, after the project tooThe clause ends with the project
Code ownershipWritten assignment and the repository transferredThey keep the repository
QAA checklist you can read"We test everything"
Time zonesHours and overlap in your time zone"We are flexible"
PricingA fixed price per scope, changes priced firstOpen-ended hourly billing
CapacityA number of parallel projects"As many as you need"
ReferencesLive sites with an honest roleOther agencies' clients on show
SecurityA vault, least access and a DPAPasswords sent by email
HandoverA written list of what you receive"We'll send the files"
DefectsScope defects fixed at their costEvery fix is billable
ExitMonthly terms and a clean handoverA long lock-in or an exit fee

Try us on one project

A partnership with SoftVolt AI starts with one real brief, not a long contract. There is no onboarding fee and no minimum, so you can judge the scope, the communication and the delivery on that project. Our partner programme page explains how it works.

See the platforms we build on and how a project runs on our white label web development service page. When you are ready, send us a brief and ask for the NDA first. You get a written scope and a fixed price within two business days.

posts.title: Next.js vs WordPress for Agency Client Sites
posts.excerpt: Next.js vs WordPress for agency client sites: a fair comparison of editing, plugins, speed, hosting, cost and SEO, and when headless WordPress fits best.
posts.content_html:
Pick WordPress when the client's team wants to build and change pages themselves, or depends on plugins. Pick Next.js when the site needs speed, custom interactions or logins, and the client accepts that layout changes go through a developer. If the client wants the WordPress admin and a faster front end, headless WordPress gives them both.

This Next.js vs WordPress guide is for agency owners deciding what to sell. We build on both, so the answer below comes from the brief, not from a preference.

What you are actually comparing

The two are different kinds of tool. WordPress is a content management system with an admin screen, a content database, themes and plugins. It runs on PHP with a MySQL or MariaDB database.

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. It has no admin screen of its own. Content either lives in the code or comes from a CMS such as WordPress, Payload or Sanity.

That difference drives most of the trade-offs below. WordPress arrives with an editor. With Next.js, you choose one, and WordPress can be that choice.

Next.js vs WordPress at a glance

FactorWordPressNext.js
EditingEditors build and change pages in the admin, with blocks or a page builderEditors fill in fields in a CMS; new layouts need a developer
PluginsOver 75,000 free plugins in the WordPress.org directory, installed from the adminPackages and APIs, wired in by a developer
PerformanceDepends on the theme, plugins, caching and hostServer Components by default, so less JavaScript reaches the browser
HostingAny PHP host that meets the WordPress requirementsA Node.js server, a Docker container or a platform such as Vercel
Cost to buildLower for brochure sites built on a theme or page builderHigher per template, because more of the site is written as code
Cost to maintainCore, plugin and theme updates, plus security monitoringFramework and package upgrades, which only a developer can do
SEOAn SEO plugin stores titles, descriptions and schemaMetadata, sitemaps and schema are set in code, route by route

The comparison, factor by factor

Editing

Editing is usually the factor that settles the brief. Some marketing teams expect to drag sections around and launch a landing page on a Friday afternoon. WordPress with blocks or Elementor suits them.

A Next.js site gives editors fields to fill in, not a blank canvas. That protects the design, but every new layout becomes a developer task. Agree that with the client before you sell the build.

Ask the client who edits the current site and what they changed last month. The answer tells you how much layout freedom they really use.

Plugins and integrations

The WordPress.org plugin directory lists over 75,000 free plugins (as listed in October 2026). Forms, bookings, memberships and shops often need no custom code at all.

That choice has a cost. Each plugin adds code to update and test, and plugins that overlap can slow a site down.

In Next.js, a developer wires in each integration, usually on the server. It takes longer, but nothing loads unless someone chose it.

Performance

In Next.js, layouts and pages are Server Components by default. The docs give less JavaScript in the browser as one reason to use them, and the server can cache the rendered result.

WordPress can be fast too. Speed comes from a lean theme, few plugins, good caching and a decent host. When we audit a slow WordPress site, we start with the build itself: add-on packs, image sizes and caching settings.

A performance pass may fix the problem for far less than a rebuild. If the client's only complaint is speed, try that first.

Hosting

WordPress runs on most PHP hosting. WordPress.org recommends PHP 8.3 or greater, MySQL 8.0 or MariaDB 10.11 or greater, and HTTPS support. Your agency may already resell hosting that meets this.

Next.js needs a different setup. The Next.js deployment docs say a Node.js server or a Docker container supports every feature, while a static export supports only some. Vercel is one of the verified platform adapters.

We deploy Next.js front ends to Vercel by default, or to the client's own infrastructure with a runbook. Either way, the hosting account stays in your name or the client's, billed at cost.

Cost to build and maintain

For a brochure site, WordPress usually costs less to build. A theme or page builder supplies much of the layout, and editors can load the content themselves. Next.js costs more per template, because more of the site is written as code.

Maintenance differs in kind. WordPress needs core, plugin and theme updates, tested on staging, plus security monitoring. Next.js needs framework and package upgrades, and a site nobody upgrades for two years becomes expensive to touch.

Agree who does that work before launch. For WordPress, a care plan with staged updates, nightly backups and uptime monitoring covers it, and you can resell it under your own brand. For Next.js, budget developer hours for upgrades every year.

On our plans, the difference shows up in the tier. Essential (from £500 a month) covers WordPress and WooCommerce builds. Next.js work starts at Growth (from £1,200 a month), and our rates page lists what each plan includes.

SEO

Both can rank well, and neither guarantees it. Search engines need clean HTML, stable URLs, metadata on every page and a sitemap, whatever produces them.

WordPress usually gets there with an SEO plugin. Next.js does it in code. The Next.js Metadata APIs generate the head tags for each page, and special files can generate the sitemap and robots.txt.

The real risk sits in rebuilds. Moving a site from WordPress to Next.js changes templates and often URLs. Every old URL needs a redirect, and every page needs its metadata carried across.

When headless WordPress gives you both

Headless WordPress splits the site in two. Editors keep the WordPress admin they know, and a Next.js front end renders what visitors see. The two talk through the WordPress REST API or the WPGraphQL plugin.

It suits a client whose WordPress site keeps failing Core Web Vitals while the team stays happy in the admin. It also suits designs that need interactions a page builder cannot deliver.

It does not suit every brief. Plugins that output front-end HTML, such as page builders and sliders, stop working, because Next.js now renders the front end. Plugins that work on data, such as ACF and SEO plugins that store metadata, keep working.

This website runs on that setup: headless WordPress with a Next.js front end on Vercel. Our headless WordPress development page explains how we build it for agencies.

A decision rule for the sales call

Ask the client these questions, in this order:

  1. Who changes the layout after launch? If the client's own team does it often, choose WordPress.
  2. Does the site need logins, dashboards or custom interactions? If yes, choose Next.js, with a CMS that suits the editors.
  3. Is the current WordPress site slow while the team likes the admin? Choose headless WordPress.
  4. Is the budget tight and the site mostly brochure pages? Choose WordPress, and spend the difference on content.

When two answers point different ways, let editing decide. A fast site the client cannot update soon goes out of date.

Three example briefs

These briefs are illustrations, not client stories. They show how the rule above plays out on typical agency work.

A local accountancy firm

The firm wants ten pages, a news section the partners update each month and a contact form. The office manager wants to add staff profiles without calling anyone.

Choose WordPress with a custom theme and ACF fields. Editors fill in a staff profile or a news post, and the design stays intact. Nothing here needs a JavaScript front end.

A property developer with a buyer portal

The developer wants filterable listings, fast mobile pages and a login where buyers track their reservation. The sales team edits listings, but rarely changes layouts.

Choose Next.js. The buyer login needs proper authentication and a data model, which suits a Next.js app on a database. The listings can come from a CMS the sales team finds easy.

A retailer with a slow WordPress site

The retailer publishes several posts a week and fails Core Web Vitals on mobile. Its marketing team has used WordPress for years and does not want to retrain.

Start with a performance audit. If the theme and plugins cannot reach the targets, choose headless WordPress. The team keeps its admin, and visitors get a faster front end.

Build either one under your brand

We build both stacks white-label, and every written scope recommends one and says why. For classic builds, see our white-label WordPress development service. For React front ends and headless builds, see white-label Next.js development.

Not sure which one the client needs? Send us the brief, and you will get a platform recommendation and a fixed-price scope within two business days.

posts.title: White Label SEO Pricing in 2026: What Agencies Pay
posts.excerpt: White label SEO pricing in 2026 from real price lists: the four pricing models, what drives cost, the margins agencies add and the red flags to avoid.
posts.content_html:
White label SEO pricing in 2026 usually means a monthly fee for each client campaign. On the public pricing pages we checked in October 2026, monthly SEO plans ran from $355 to $2,219. One UK-facing provider puts most UK packages at £400 to £1,200 per client per month.

The headline number tells you less than the pricing model, the scope behind it and how openly the provider shows its work. This guide covers each of those, with a worked margin example and the red flags to check before you sign.

White label SEO pricing at a glance

These prices come from each provider's own pricing page, as listed in October 2026. We quote them as neutral market reference points. Check the live page before you budget, because providers change prices and terms.

Provider and planListed pricePricing modelNotes from the page
SEOReseller pricing and packages: Local SEO$499 per client, billed monthlyPer campaign, monthlyNo contracts for your clients, and a 30-day notice period if your agency stops using them entirely
SEOReseller: National SEO$699 per client, billed monthlyPer campaign, monthlyWhite-labelled reporting on every client campaign
SEOReseller: GBP Only$299 per client, billed monthlyPer campaign, monthlyA Google Business Profile plan, priced apart from full SEO
Agency Platform SEO plans: Starter to Platinum$355 to $2,219 a monthTiered monthly plansShown at its Gold Membership rate; tiers rise from 10 to 75 primary focus keywords
Uplers white label marketing services$25 to $40 an hourPer hourA general rate across its white label marketing work, with 10% extra for Australian or Singapore hours and 20% extra for US time-zone support
BrightLocal Citation BuilderFrom $2 per citationPer deliverableUnbranded reports that agencies can present as their own

These providers list their prices in US dollars, so we have left them in dollars. SEOReseller states plainly that it does not guarantee results, which is the honest position for any SEO provider.

The four pricing models, and when each one fits

Most white label SEO providers sell on one of four models. Each one moves risk between you and the provider in a different way.

ModelHow you paySuitsWatch for
Per campaign, monthlyA fixed fee per client each monthOngoing SEO retainers that you resell month after monthVague inclusions, such as "on-page optimisation" with no page count
Per hourLogged hours at an agreed rateTechnical backlogs and work of uncertain sizeOpen-ended hours with no estimate or cap
Per deliverableA unit price per citation, article or auditTopping up a retainer with extra outputBuying volume when the client needs a plan
Revenue shareA percentage of what you bill the clientTesting a new service with little cash up frontThe provider sees your client pricing, and its fee rises when yours does

Per campaign, monthly

Both SEO price lists in the table use this model. SEOReseller prices each client campaign monthly, and Agency Platform sells tiers that rise with the number of keywords and content pieces.

It works because your client also pays you monthly, so cost and revenue line up. Ask for the inclusions in numbers: pages optimised, content pieces, links earned and the report each month.

Per hour

Hourly pricing suits work that is hard to size in advance, such as clearing a technical audit across many page templates. Uplers lists $25 to $40 an hour across its white label marketing services, and charges more for Australian or US hours.

With hourly billing, the risk sits with you, because hours can run on. Ask for an estimate per task and a cap that needs your approval before anyone goes past it.

Per deliverable

Some SEO work comes in clean units. BrightLocal's Citation Builder, for example, starts at $2 per citation and includes unbranded reports.

Unit pricing makes cost easy to forecast. It does not decide what the client needs, though. Someone still has to choose which pages get content and which listings matter.

Revenue share

With revenue share, the provider takes an agreed percentage of what you charge the client. None of the pricing pages we opened published a rate, so treat any offer as a negotiation.

It lowers your risk on a new service. The trade-off is that the provider needs to know your client pricing. The deal also gets harder to unwind once several clients sit on it.

What drives the price

Two plans with the same price can hide very different amounts of work. These factors move the number most.

  • Keywords and pages in scope. Agency Platform's tiers climb from 10 to 75 primary focus keywords, and from one to four content pieces.
  • Local or national targeting. SEOReseller lists national SEO at $200 a month more than local SEO.
  • Content and links. In our experience, writing and outreach take the most hours in a retainer. Ask how many pieces and placements a month the fee covers.
  • Technical work. The platform, the number of page templates and whether fixes need code all change the effort. A WordPress settings change and a Shopify theme edit are different jobs.
  • Locations and languages. Each extra location or language adds research, pages and tracking.
  • Time zone and communication. Live overlap with your team costs more with some providers, as the Uplers surcharges show.
  • Reporting and account management. A named contact and a report in your template take real time, and the price should reflect it.

When you compare quotes, put them in a table with the same rows: keywords, pages, content, links, reporting and notice period. The cheapest line often turns out to include the least.

Margins: what agencies add on top

Most of the pages we opened leave retail pricing to you. Agency Platform says you control retail pricing and keep the markup, and SEOReseller gives no suggested retail price.

Only one page gave a margin figure. ROI Minds' guide to white label SEO in the UK advises a target gross margin of 60% to 70% on every retainer.

The same page treats a margin under 50% as a sign that provider costs are too high or the retainer is underpriced. That is one provider's guidance, not an industry survey, so test it against your own costs.

Worked example: margin versus markup

Margin and markup often get mixed up, and the mix-up costs money. Say your white label provider charges £600 a month for one client campaign.

  • You charge the client £1,500, so your gross profit is £900.
  • Your margin is £900 ÷ £1,500, which is 60%.
  • Your markup is £900 ÷ £600, which is 150%.
  • If you "add 60%" to the £600 cost instead, you charge £960. Your margin is then only 37.5%.

A simple rule: retail price equals cost divided by (1 minus your target margin). For a 60% margin on £600, that is £600 ÷ 0.4, or £1,500.

Your margin also has to pay for your own team. Count the account manager's calls, the report reviews and the client's questions before you set the retail price.

Red flags in white label SEO pricing

A low price is not a red flag on its own. These are, at any price.

  • Guaranteed rankings.Google's guidance on hiring an SEO says nobody can guarantee a number one ranking on Google. A provider that promises positions is guessing, or using tactics that put your client's site at risk.
  • Unexplained link packages. "20 links a month" with no list of sites is a warning sign. Google's same guidance tells site owners to avoid SEOs who talk about link popularity schemes. Ask for every placement with its URL and date.
  • Secretive methods. Google also warns against SEOs who will not clearly explain what they plan to do. If the provider cannot tell you what changed on the site this month, your report cannot either.
  • Reports with rankings and nothing else. A report should show the work done. Positions alone can move for reasons outside anyone's control.
  • Long lock-ins on a first contract. SEOReseller and Agency Platform both list month-to-month or short-notice terms. A 12-month minimum before you have seen any work puts all the risk on you.
  • Accounts the provider owns. If the provider holds the Search Console, GA4 or reporting accounts, you lose the history when you leave. Keep them in the client's name or your agency's.

How we price white label SEO at SoftVolt AI

We price ongoing SEO on a monthly plan and quote one-off work separately. Ongoing SEO sits in our Premium plan, from £2,400 a month, and in Enterprise, which we quote.

Essential and Growth cover website builds, so SEO starts at Premium. Premium covers up to 6 active projects at a time across builds, AI automation, SEO and paid media. It includes a named producer and same-day priority support.

One-off work, such as implementing a technical audit, gets a written scope and a fixed price within two business days. The cost depends on the URLs and templates involved, the platform and how many fixes need code. Our technical SEO implementation page explains that work.

Plans are monthly with no lock-in. We bill tools and other third-party costs at cost, with no mark-up, or you hold them in your own accounts. Every plan is on the rates page.

posts.title: How to White Label a Headless WordPress Build
posts.excerpt: Headless WordPress for agencies, step by step: content model, WPGraphQL or REST, preview, revalidation, hosting, SEO and a handover under your own brand.
posts.content_html:
To white-label a headless WordPress build, agree the content model and choose WPGraphQL or the REST API. Then wire up preview and revalidation, and finish with hosting, SEO and a handover under your agency's name.

Editors keep the WordPress admin, and visitors get a Next.js front end. Your client never meets the partner.

Headless WordPress for agencies works best when each of these steps is written into the scope. Each one hides a decision your client will notice after launch.

What headless WordPress for agencies involves

WordPress stays where editors write and publish. A separate Next.js front end fetches that content and renders every page visitors see, so visitors never touch the WordPress install.

We know this setup from building it and from running on it. Before SoftVolt AI, our founder built The Bulk Bag Man, a site for a UK aggregates supplier, this way. Our own site, softvoltai.com, runs on headless WordPress with a Next.js App Router front end on Vercel.

The steps below follow the order we work in.

Step 1: Agree the content model

Decide what editors fill in before anyone writes a template. A headless front end only shows the fields you expose, so a missing field turns into a developer task later.

  • One ACF field group per template, with the fields that template needs and nothing more.
  • Custom post types for repeating content. The Bulk Bag Man exposes a Supplies post type.
  • Menus and site settings exposed to the front end, because the header and footer depend on them.
  • Only public data leaving WordPress, so drafts and private fields stay inside.
  • A list of every plugin, with a note on whether it still works headless.

That last point catches agencies out. Plugins that output front-end HTML, such as page builders and sliders, stop working. Plugins that work on data, such as ACF and SEO plugins that store metadata, keep working.

We list each plugin in the scope and say what replaces it. You can then explain the change to your client before they find it.

Step 2: Choose WPGraphQL or the REST API

Both work, and we have used both. The right choice depends on how much each page asks for at once.

The WordPress REST API comes with WordPress. It sends and receives data as JSON, and any language that can make HTTP requests can use it. Each endpoint returns a set shape, so a busy page may need several requests.

WPGraphQL is a free, open-source plugin that adds a GraphQL API to WordPress. Its introduction to GraphQL explains that you ask for exactly the fields you want, and one request can replace many round trips.

QuestionREST APIWPGraphQL
Extra plugin to maintain?No, it comes with WordPressYes, one more plugin to update and test
Data per requestA set shape per endpointExactly the fields the query asks for
Draft previewsA custom route you write and controlSupported, for requests authenticated as an editor
Where it fits bestSmaller sites with a few templatesSites with many templates and related content

The Bulk Bag Man uses the REST API. A WordPress child theme exposes its ACF fields, menus and the Supplies post type. A Next.js App Router front end renders them on Vercel.

Our own site has more than a dozen content types, from services to case studies, and reads them all through WPGraphQL.

Plan forms at the same time. On The Bulk Bag Man, contact form submissions go through a Next.js route handler, so the browser never talks to WordPress directly.

Step 3: Make preview work for editors

Editors expect the Preview button to show their draft on the real site. In a headless build, that needs deliberate work on both sides.

On the Next.js side, Draft Mode handles it. WordPress opens a route handler with a shared secret, and the handler sets a Draft Mode cookie and redirects to the page. That browser then skips the cache, while other visitors still see the cached page.

On the WordPress side, something has to return the draft. WPGraphQL previews need the request to be authenticated as a user who can edit the post.

On softvoltai.com we took a different route. A read-only REST endpoint takes the shared secret and a post ID and returns that one post, including the newest autosave. The front end never holds a login that can write.

Test preview with a real editor before launch. Ask them to change a draft, preview it, publish it and check the live page. If any of those steps confuses them, fix it before your client sees it.

Step 4: Revalidate on publish

A headless front end serves cached pages, so the live site changes only when something tells Next.js to refresh. Get this wrong and your client publishes a price change that does not appear.

The Next.js revalidation docs describe two on-demand tools. revalidatePath drops one route, and revalidateTag drops every cached entry with a given tag. The docs prefer tags where possible, because they are more precise.

On our own site, a publish runs like this:

  1. An editor saves, publishes or deletes a post in WordPress.
  2. A small plugin works out which front-end paths and cache tags that post affects.
  3. The plugin posts them to a Next.js route handler, with a shared secret in the header.
  4. The route handler checks the secret and drops exactly those paths and tags.
  5. The next visitor gets the new page, and every other page stays cached.

One detail matters. The docs recommend a profile for revalidateTag that keeps serving the old page while the new one builds. We expire the tag at once on publish instead, because editors check their change straight away.

Menu and settings changes refresh every page, since the header and footer appear everywhere. An admin bar button also rebuilds the whole front end for the rare page that looks stale.

Step 5: Decide hosting and account ownership

A headless build has two hosts. The Next.js front end runs on Vercel by default, or on the client's own infrastructure. WordPress stays on its existing host, or moves to a new one, and stops serving visitors directly.

Put both accounts in your agency's name or the client's from day one. We bill hosting at cost or set it up in your account with no mark-up. Nothing depends on an account we keep.

Lock the CMS domain down as well. On our install, visitors to the WordPress domain go to the real site instead. The domain stays out of search indexes, while the admin, the APIs and previews keep working.

Step 6: Cover the SEO basics

A headless site can rank as well as any other, provided the rebuild carries the SEO work across. Next.js renders pages on the server, so search engines receive complete HTML. The rest is a checklist:

  • A title, description and canonical tag for every route, drawn from the WordPress fields.
  • An XML sitemap built from the published content.
  • Structured data, validated before launch.
  • A redirect from every old URL that changes.
  • The WordPress domain kept out of the index, so the same content never appears on two hosts.
  • Staging protected by a password and set to noindex.

We do not promise rankings. A clean technical base removes the problems that hold a rebuilt site back, and the rest depends on content and links.

Step 7: Hand over under your agency's brand

Handover is where white label holds or fails. Your client may open the repository, the theme files or the hosting dashboard, and each one should show your agency or nobody.

  • Commit messages, staging domains and documents carry your brand from the first day.
  • Theme and plugin headers name your agency, with no footer credit or "built by" line.
  • An editing guide in your brand shows where each WordPress field appears on the site.
  • The Git repository transfers to you or the client, along with hosting and CMS access.
  • A runbook documents any deployment on the client's own infrastructure.
  • Our access is revoked, and we confirm the removal in writing.

We sign a mutual NDA before the brief and never contact your client. Credentials live in a shared vault with least-privilege access, and our security page sets out each practice.

Where to start

Headless builds are included from our Growth plan, from £1,200 a month. It covers up to 3 active projects and up to 10 pages per project, and larger rebuilds get their own fixed-price scope.

Our headless WordPress development service covers this pattern. If the client needs a different CMS, such as Payload or Sanity, see white-label Next.js development.

Send us the brief with the current site URL and the client's plugin list. You will get a written scope with a fixed price within two business days.

posts.title: In-house vs Freelancer vs White-Label Partner: Real Costs
posts.excerpt: White label vs in house developer costs, worked out from BLS, HMRC and pension rules, plus where a freelancer fits and when a monthly plan pays off.
posts.primary_keyword: white label vs in house developer
posts.content_html:
Agency owners who search "white label vs in house developer" usually want one number. In the UK, an experienced web developer on £60,000 costs about £69,571 a year. That includes employer National Insurance and the minimum workplace pension, but not a laptop, software or a recruiter's fee.

A freelancer costs their day rate multiplied by the days you use, and our white-label plans start at £500 a month. The three options buy different things, so below we show every sum with its source and then give a rule for choosing.

What an in-house web developer costs in the UK

The National Careers Service web developer profile lists an average salary of £27,000 for a starter and £60,000 for an experienced developer. Typical hours are 37 to 39 a week, and we read the figures in October 2026.

On top of salary, the law sets two costs for every employer:

  • Employer National Insurance. Employers pay 15% on earnings above the secondary threshold of £5,000 a year in 2026 to 2027. The figures come from HMRC's rates and thresholds for employers.
  • Workplace pension. Employers must pay at least 3% of earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 in 2026/27. See The Pensions Regulator's guide to contributions.

The Employment Allowance (£10,500 for 2026 to 2027) can cut your total employer National Insurance bill if your business qualifies. It applies to your whole payroll rather than one hire, so our sums leave it out.

For the experienced developer, National Insurance is 15% of £55,000 (£60,000 minus £5,000), which is £8,250. The pension is 3% of £44,030 (£50,270 minus £6,240), which is £1,320.90. The total comes to £69,570.90 a year, or about £5,798 a month.

For the starter, National Insurance is 15% of £22,000, which is £3,300. The pension is 3% of £20,760, which is £622.80. The total is £30,922.80 a year, or about £2,577 a month.

What an in-house web developer costs in the US

The Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook puts the median annual wage for web developers at $92,650 in May 2025. The lowest 10% earned less than $48,100 and the highest 10% more than $162,290.

US employers also pay benefits on top of wages. The BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation table for private industry shows the split by type of job.

In June 2026, wages made up 69.2% of total compensation for professional and related occupations, and benefits made up 30.8%. Those benefits cover paid leave, supplemental pay, insurance, retirement and legally required benefits.

Apply that split to the median wage and the total is about $133,887 a year ($92,650 divided by 0.692). That works out at about $11,157 a month.

This is an average for a broad group of jobs, not a quote for one developer. Still, it shows the scale: each dollar of salary brings roughly 45 cents of benefits.

White label vs in house developer: the yearly numbers side by side

This table puts the hires next to a freelancer and our plans. Read the assumptions under it before you quote any line to a colleague.

OptionBase costEmployer on-costsPer yearPer month
UK hire, starter£27,000 salary£3,300 National Insurance and £622.80 pension£30,923£2,577
UK hire, experienced£60,000 salary£8,250 National Insurance and £1,320.90 pension£69,571£5,798
US hire, median wage$92,650 wagesAbout $41,237 in benefitsAbout $133,887About $11,157
FreelancerDay rate multiplied by days usedNone for youDepends on useDepends on use
SoftVolt AI EssentialFrom £500 a monthNoneFrom £6,000From £500
SoftVolt AI GrowthFrom £1,200 a monthNoneFrom £14,400From £1,200
SoftVolt AI PremiumFrom £2,400 a monthNoneFrom £28,800From £2,400
SoftVolt AI EnterpriseQuotedNoneQuotedQuoted

Assumptions behind the table

  • UK salaries are the National Careers Service starter and experienced figures for a web developer.
  • UK National Insurance uses the standard 15% rate above £5,000 for 2026 to 2027, with no Employment Allowance.
  • The UK pension is the 3% legal minimum. Many employers pay more.
  • US wages are the BLS median for web developers in May 2025. Benefits use the June 2026 share for private-industry professional and related occupations.
  • Plan prices are SoftVolt AI's "from" prices in pounds. We have not converted them to dollars.
  • The table leaves out equipment, software, recruitment, office space, training and your management time. No official source prices these for a web developer, and each one adds to the cost of a hire.

What each option buys

The table compares price, not output. A full-time hire gives you one person for every working day.

A freelancer gives you the days you book. A plan gives you a set number of projects running in parallel, with page limits per project and a set turnaround:

  • Essential, from £500 a month: 1 active project, WordPress and WooCommerce, up to 5 pages, 10 to 15 business days.
  • Growth, from £1,200 a month: up to 3 active projects, adds headless Next.js, up to 10 pages, 7 to 10 business days and a named producer.
  • Premium, from £2,400 a month: up to 6 active projects, adds AI automation, SEO and paid media, up to 15 pages, 5 to 7 business days.
  • Enterprise, quoted: unlimited active projects and turnaround agreed in writing.

Work outside a plan, such as a migration, gets its own written scope and fixed price first. The other differences show up in day-to-day running:

FactorIn-house hireFreelancerWhite-label partner
Time to startWeeks or months to advertise, interview and onboardWhenever someone good is freeA written scope and fixed price within two business days
Who manages the workYou doYou doA named producer in your shared channel
Holidays and sick daysDelivery pausesYou find a replacement mid-projectTeam cover, with the same producer on the thread
If it does not work outNotice periods and a new searchLost time and a scramble for files and loginsWork ends at handover, with documentation and credentials returned

The cost the table cannot show: quiet months

An employee costs the same in a quiet month as in a busy one. Suppose your build work fills a developer for only six months of the year. Each busy month of the experienced UK hire then costs about £11,595 (£69,571 divided by 6).

A freelancer and a monthly plan both shrink when work drops. You stop booking days, or you move a plan down, because our plans run month to month with no long-term contract.

Where a freelancer fits

Use a break-even rule. Divide the monthly cost of the hire you are weighing by the days of work you actually have that month.

Take the experienced UK hire at £5,798 a month. With 10 days of build work, a freelancer breaks even at about £580 a day. With 15 days, the figure falls to about £387.

Below that rate the freelancer costs less on paper. You still manage the work, cover their holidays and check the quality yourself.

A freelancer suits one small job you can supervise. For a pipeline of builds with dates you have promised to clients, a team with cover and a written scope carries less risk.

Run the sums for your own agency

Our table uses public averages. Your own figures will differ, so rebuild it with these steps:

  1. Take the salary you would actually offer, not the national average.
  2. Add employer National Insurance at 15% of everything above £5,000.
  3. Add your pension scheme's employer rate, at least 3% of earnings between £6,240 and £50,270.
  4. Add quotes for a laptop, software licences and a recruiter's fee.
  5. Count the months a year you could keep that person busy on billable builds.
  6. Divide the total by those months, then compare the result with a plan price or a freelancer's monthly bill.

If the busy-month cost of a hire comes out well above a plan price, outsourcing is likely cheaper. If your pipeline keeps a developer busy every month, a hire may be the better deal.

A simple rule for choosing

  • Hire in-house when you have steady, full-time work on one stack all year.
  • Book a freelancer for a small, well-defined job you have time to manage.
  • Use a white-label partner when build volume rises and falls, or when a brief needs a platform your team does not use.

Many agencies mix them. They keep one developer in-house for small changes and send larger builds, or unfamiliar platforms, to a partner.

Price your next build

See what our team builds on the white-label web development page, and the design side on the white-label web design page. Every plan and pricing term sits on our rates page.

The quickest way to compare is with a real brief. Send us one and you get a written scope with a fixed price within two business days. Set it against your own hiring sums.

posts.title: AI Automation Services Agencies Can Resell Safely
posts.excerpt: AI automation for agencies: five services you can resell, how to price them honestly, UK GDPR rules for client data, and where AI is the wrong tool.
posts.content_html:
Agencies can safely resell five AI services: lead routing, reporting automation, AI chat on client websites, on-site voice agents and content workflows. Each one works when you scope it as a single measurable task and a person approves anything a customer sees.

This guide to AI automation for agencies covers what to sell and how to price it. It then covers UK GDPR for client data sent to AI APIs. Last come the jobs where we tell agencies to leave AI out.

AI automation for agencies: five services you can resell

Each service below replaces a job your client already pays someone to do by hand. That makes the value easy to explain and easy to measure.

1. Lead routing and qualification

The automation reads each enquiry from the website form, the inbox or the ad platform. It scores the lead against the client's criteria, sends it to the right person and drafts a first reply for approval.

Most of this is plain rules work. The AI step only reads free text, for example to decide whether a message is a sales enquiry, a complaint or spam. Our workflow automation service covers the rules side.

2. Reporting automation

The workflow pulls last month's figures from the ad platforms and analytics into a sheet before the account manager opens it. A model then drafts commentary on those figures, and the account manager edits it.

The AI never calculates a number. Code does the maths, and the model only describes what the code produced.

3. AI chat on client websites

An on-site assistant answers visitor questions from the client's own pages, policies and product data, and shows where each answer came from. When the content does not cover a topic, it says so and hands the visitor to a person.

Sell it as a way to cut repeat questions for the client's team. Do not sell it as a replacement for their staff. Our AI assistants and chat page explains how we test these builds before launch.

4. Voice agents on WordPress sites

A voice agent lets visitors talk to the website instead of typing. Our own SoftVolt AI Voice Agent plugin is free on WordPress.org and does this today. It answers from the facts you give it, books services and sends each lead by email, Telegram or an n8n webhook.

Speech runs in the visitor's browser, so voice adds no cost. Only the text of the conversation goes to the AI provider.

Be clear with clients about one limit. White label and agency mode are planned for the plugin's Pro add-on, which is not available yet. If a client needs a fully unbranded agent now, we scope a custom build under your brand instead.

It is also an on-site agent, not a phone line, so do not sell it as a call answering service.

5. Content workflows

A content workflow drafts product descriptions, meta descriptions or social captions from a sheet of facts the client supplies. An editor signs off every item before it goes live.

The value sits in the structure: consistent fields, the client's tone rules and a clear approval step. Without an editor in the loop, you are reselling risk.

Which service fits which client

Use this table in the sales conversation. If the client cannot supply what the third column asks for, the service is not ready to sell yet.

ServiceGood fit whenWhat you need from the clientMain risk to manage
Lead routingLeads land in several inboxes and replies are slowLead criteria, owners and a batch of past enquiriesA reply sent under the client's name without approval
Reporting automationAccount managers spend hours collecting figures each monthRead access to the ad, analytics and CRM accountsA model stating a figure the data does not support
AI chatVisitors ask the same questions every dayApproved pages, policies and product dataOut-of-date content, and personal details typed into the chat
Voice agent on WordPressA service or WooCommerce site wants bookings outside office hoursServices, prices and the details to collect before bookingPromising white label before it exists
Content workflowThe client publishes many similar itemsA clean product sheet and written tone rulesPublishing without an editor's sign-off

How to price and package AI automation honestly

Price each automation as three separate lines: a fixed setup fee, a monthly run fee and AI usage at cost. Clients understand the split, and a busy month no longer eats your margin.

  • Setup: a fixed price for one defined task, including the test set and the approval flow.
  • Monthly run fee: monitoring, re-running the tests when a prompt or model changes, and a usage report.
  • Usage: model and tool costs passed through at cost, or billed to an API account in the client's name.

Agree the measure before you build. Time the task as it runs today, then report the same measure after launch. Do not promise a deflection rate, a conversion lift or hours saved until you have the client's own data.

A worked example: lead routing for a trades client

Say a plumbing firm gets enquiries through a web form, email and Meta lead forms, and replies within a day at best. The proposal covers one automation, written like this.

  1. Scope: route every enquiry to the CRM within minutes, tag it (emergency, quote request, existing customer or spam) and draft a reply.
  2. Guardrail: the office manager approves every drafted reply before it goes out.
  3. Test set: 50 past enquiries with the tag the office manager would have chosen, re-run on every change.
  4. Measure: median time to first reply, taken for two weeks before launch and every month after.
  5. Costs: a fixed setup fee, a fixed run fee and AI usage on the client's own API account.

Nothing in that proposal relies on a number you cannot check later. That makes it easy to renew.

If you resell our work, AI automation sits in our Premium plan, from £2,400 a month for up to 6 active projects. It is also in Enterprise, which is quoted. A one-off automation gets a written scope and a fixed price within two business days of the brief.

Client data, AI APIs and UK GDPR

When an automation sends a customer's enquiry to a model provider, personal data leaves your client's systems. Under UK GDPR, check four things before launch: roles and contracts, the impact assessment, the fields you send and the transfer.

Work out who is controller and who is processor

Your client is normally the controller of its customers' data. The ICO's guidance on accountability and governance in AI covers the provider's role. A provider acting only on a client's instructions is likely to be a processor, even if it makes some technical decisions.

Your agency, a white-label partner and the model provider then form a chain of processors. The ICO lists what a controller and processor contract must include.

One rule matters most here: a processor needs the controller's prior written authorisation before it uses a sub-processor. So name the model provider in the data processing agreement before anything goes live.

Expect to need a DPIA

The same AI guidance says the vast majority of AI uses involve processing likely to result in a high risk. That triggers a data protection impact assessment. If you decide a use is not high risk, the ICO says you still need to document how you reached that view.

Send only the fields the task needs

The ICO's page on security and data minimisation in AI asks you to identify the minimum personal data you need. It also says you must not collect personal data in case it proves useful later.

For lead tagging, the model rarely needs a phone number or a surname. Strip them out before the API call, and add them back when the result returns.

Check the transfer and the provider's terms

If the model provider processes data outside the UK, the transfer rules apply. The ICO's brief guide to international transfers sets them out. Every restricted transfer needs adequacy regulations, safeguards such as the IDTA or the Addendum, or an exception.

Then read the provider's own data terms. OpenAI's enterprise privacy page says it does not train on business data by default. It may keep API inputs and outputs for up to 30 days.

Anthropic's privacy centre says it does not train on data from its commercial products, unless the customer joins its Development Partner Program. Whichever provider you pick, keep a copy of its data terms with the data processing agreement.

The ICO marks its AI and processor contract guidance as under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act. Check both again before each new project.

On our side, Bangladesh is not on the EU adequacy list. We work under the UK IDTA or Addendum, EU SCCs and an Article 28 agreement, as our security page sets out.

Where AI is a poor fit

Some of the most useful advice you can give a client is to skip the AI step. We say so in the scope when a brief falls into one of these groups.

  • Rules you can write down. Moving, checking and deduplicating data is cheaper and more predictable in plain code.
  • Exact figures. Prices, VAT, quotes and totals belong in code. A model can describe a number, but it should never produce one.
  • Advice a customer acts on alone. Legal, medical or financial answers need a qualified person, so the assistant refuses and hands over.
  • Rare tasks. A job done twice a month rarely repays the build and the monitoring.
  • Thin or stale content. An assistant is only as accurate as the pages it reads, so fix the content first.
  • Decisions about people. Keep a person in charge of anything that seriously affects someone, such as a refused refund or a job application.

A simple decision rule helps here. If the client cannot give you 30 real examples with the right answer, the task is not ready. Nobody could test the result.

Reselling AI automation under your brand

You keep the client, the pricing and the decision about what the AI may do. We design, build and test the automation behind your agency, and our name appears nowhere.

We sign a mutual NDA before you share the brief, and we never contact your client. A named producer runs each project, and we fix post-launch defects inside the agreed scope at our cost.

See how we scope this work on our white-label AI automation page. When you have a task in mind, send us the brief with a few real examples. We reply with a fixed-price scope within two business days.
