posts.excerpt: White label SEO reporting that clients read: what a monthly report needs from Search Console and GA4, how to brand it and how to report a bad month.
posts.content_html:
Good white label SEO reporting answers four questions each month. What changed in Google Search, and what did that lead to on the site? What work did the team do, and what comes next?

Send the report monthly under your agency's brand, with Search Console and GA4 as the data sources. Put a plain-English summary on page one, so a busy client gets the point without scrolling.

What white label SEO reporting should contain

We build monthly reports around the sections below. Each section has one source, so nobody argues about where a number came from.

SectionSourceWhat to show
SummaryYour account managerThree to five sentences on what moved, why it moved and the plan
Search visibilitySearch ConsoleClicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position, month on month and year on year
Results on the siteGA4Organic sessions and key events, such as enquiries or sales
RankingsSearch Console or your rank trackerTracked queries grouped by topic, with the page that ranks for each
Work completedThe change logEach change with its page, date and reason
Links earnedThe change logEach placement with its URL and date
Next monthThe agreed planTasks in priority order, plus anything you need from the client

This mirrors the monthly report from our white-label SEO service. It covers Search Console and GA4 data, the work completed, links earned and next month's plan.

Keep the order the same every month. Clients learn where to look, and a missing section stands out straight away.

Search Console: what happened before the click

Search Console records how the site performs in Google Search itself. Google's guide to using Search Console and Google Analytics data together calls Search Console the source of truth for Search performance.

The Search Console Performance report gives four numbers: clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position. You can break each one down by query, page, country, device, search appearance and date.

Two details confuse clients, so explain them once in the report.

  • Average position averages the top spot. Google records the topmost position a link to the site held for each query, then averages that across all queries. When the site starts to appear for new, lower-ranked queries, the average can fall while clicks rise.
  • The newest data can change. Google marks the most recent data in the Performance report as preliminary, and it may change over the next few hours. Pull the report after the month has closed, not on its last day.

AI Overviews show up in these numbers too. A click on an external link in an AI Overview counts as a click. All the links in one overview share a single position.

Chart and table totals can also differ. The chart counts by property, while the page table counts each URL separately.

GA4: what happened after the click

GA4 shows what organic visitors did once they reached the site. The figure that matters most is GA4 key events: actions that Google describes as most important to the business. For most clients, that means a form, a call or a sale.

Report organic sessions and key events side by side, filtered to Google organic traffic. Google's own example dashboard filters to session source "google" and session medium "organic", which makes a sensible default.

Search Console clicks will never match GA4 sessions exactly. Google's guide gives the main reasons:

  • Clicks and sessions are counted differently.
  • Search Console reports only the canonical URL, while GA4 reports any URL that carries the tag.
  • Search Console uses Pacific Time, while GA4 uses the time zone you set.
  • GA4 excludes known bots automatically, and Search Console does not necessarily filter them out.
  • Visitors who opt out of tracking can skew GA4 figures.

Add one line to the report saying the two tools measure different things, and compare trends rather than totals. Google gives the same advice and treats small gaps as normal.

If the GA4 numbers themselves are in doubt, fix the tracking before you report on it. Our GA4 and conversion tracking service audits the property and Tag Manager container first. The report then starts from data the client can trust.

Rankings, without the panic

Clients like rankings because they are easy to read. Rankings are also often the most volatile number in the report.

Group tracked queries by topic and show how many sit in positions 1 to 3, 4 to 10 and 11 to 20. A move between those bands means more than one keyword slipping two places.

Always name the page that ranks, so the client can link each result to the work behind it. If you use a separate rank tracker, state the location and device it checks from. Otherwise the client searches from their office, sees a different result and stops trusting the report.

The work log builds trust

Google's guidance on hiring an SEO suggests asking whether the SEO will share all the changes it makes to the site. A white label report should answer that before the client thinks to ask.

For technical fixes, we keep a change log for each site, written to go straight into the client report. Each line gives the page, what changed and the date. Links go in the same log with their URLs.

The log protects you as well. If the client's own team edits a page and undoes a change, the log shows what moved and when.

Branding: your report, your name

A white label report carries your logo, colours, fonts and template. Check the places people forget: file names, PDF document properties, dashboard titles and the sending address.

If you report in Looker Studio, build the dashboard on data sources that the client or your agency owns. It then keeps working if you change providers, and your team can edit it without anyone's help.

Access matters too. A Search Console owner can add users at different permission levels, and a restricted user gets view rights on most data. Give a reporting partner the lowest level that does the job, and keep ownership with the client.

Cadence: monthly reports, quarterly reviews

In our experience, weekly SEO reports mostly show day-to-day noise, so a monthly report suits most retainers. Add other touchpoints around it as the account needs them.

  • Monthly: the full report, sent in the first week of the next month once the data has settled.
  • Quarterly: a review call with year-on-year comparisons and a fresh look at priorities.
  • Weekly, for a short spell: during a migration, a relaunch or a sudden drop, when the client needs to see someone watching.

Keep the date ranges the same every month. Switching the comparison period to flatter a result is the quickest way to lose a client's trust.

Honesty when the numbers go down

Every SEO account has flat or falling months. The report should say so on page one, in plain words.

A good summary for a bad month names the drop, gives the likely cause and sets out the next step. Here is an example with made-up figures:

Organic clicks fell 12% on last month, mostly because two blog posts lost positions after a Google update. Enquiries from organic search held steady. This month we will refresh both posts and add internal links to them from the service pages.

The example states the number and gives a cause the client can check. It also avoids promising a recovery date, because Google decides rankings and no honest report promises positions.

Report good months the same way. Name the work that probably caused the gain, and say so when the cause is unclear.

What to leave out

A longer report is not a better report. Cut anything the client cannot act on, or that you would struggle to explain on a call.

  • Raw keyword lists. Hundreds of tracked terms with no clicks bury the few that matter. Show topics and the biggest movers instead.
  • Third-party authority scores as goals. SEO tool vendors calculate these scores themselves. Report the links earned, with their URLs, instead.
  • Charts with no explanation. A chart with no sentence under it leaves the client to guess. Give every chart one line that says what it shows.
  • Every small task. List meaningful changes in the work log. Group small edits, such as twenty image alt text updates, into one line.

How we produce white label SEO reports

When we run SEO for an agency, the monthly report goes to you first. It uses your template, or a Looker Studio dashboard built to match it.

You review it, add your own commentary and send it as your own. Our name appears nowhere, including file names and document properties, and we never contact your client.

Every change and link in the report comes from the log our team works from, so the report always matches the work. Fixes from our technical SEO team go into the same log.

Get reports your clients will read

If you resell SEO and want reports under your own brand, start with our white-label SEO services. Send a brief through our contact page, and we will return a written scope and a fixed price within two business days.

posts.title: Laravel Developer for Hire vs a White-Label Laravel Team
posts.excerpt: Laravel developer for hire, dedicated developer or white-label team? Compare cover, code ownership, testing, handover and cost structure for agencies.
posts.content_html:
A Laravel developer for hire suits a small, well-defined job that someone on your team can manage and review. A white-label Laravel team suits client applications that need cover, testing and a clean handover under your agency's name.

A dedicated developer sits between the two: steady capacity, but still one person. This guide compares all three on the points that cause trouble later, from code ownership to how you pay.

Laravel developer for hire, dedicated developer or white-label team

The three models differ in who manages the work and who carries the risk when something breaks. Here is what each one means in this guide.

  • Freelance Laravel developer for hire: an individual who bills by the hour, day or project and works for several clients.
  • Dedicated developer: one developer who works only on your projects, either on your payroll or contracted monthly through a staffing firm.
  • White-label Laravel team: a company that builds the app behind your agency to a written scope, under your brand.

How the three models compare

The table covers the questions agencies tend to ask only after a project goes wrong. Ask them before you sign instead.

What mattersFreelancerDedicated developerWhite-label team
Who manages the workYou doYou do, day to dayA named producer in your shared channel
Holidays and sicknessYou find a replacement mid-projectDelivery pauses unless the firm supplies coverTeam cover, with the same producer on the thread
Code ownershipNeeds a written assignment in the contractUsually yours if you employ them. With a staffing firm, check the contractTransferred to you or your client at handover, as agreed in writing
TestingDepends on the individualDepends on the individual and the standards you setAgreed in the scope, with tests run before each deploy
HandoverOften a scramble for files and loginsKnowledge sits with one personRepository, runbook and environment notes, with access revoked
Cost structureA time-based rate, plus your own review hoursSalary and employer costs, or a monthly fee, whether or not there is workA fixed price per scope, or a monthly plan
ConfidentialityYour client's app may end up in their portfolioInternal, or covered by the firm's termsMutual NDA, no contact with your client, no credit anywhere

Cover: who answers when the developer is away

Cover is where single-person models break first. A freelancer may take a better-paid job mid-project, and a dedicated developer still takes holidays and gets ill.

Ask every provider one question. If the developer is off for two weeks, who answers the client's bug report?

With a staffing firm, also ask whether it supplies a stand-in and who briefs them. A stand-in who has never seen the code needs time to learn it.

With us, the answer is the named producer on your project, with the rest of the team behind them. We work from Dhaka (UTC+6), so a brief sent at 5pm London can be in review by 9am.

Code ownership: get it in writing

Ownership is easy to overlook until a client asks for the code. For UK agencies, the government's guidance on ownership of copyright works sets the default. An employer is usually the first owner of work an employee creates in the course of employment.

Under a contract for services, such as a freelance job, the creator usually keeps the copyright unless a contract says otherwise. So with a freelancer, put a written assignment of the code in the contract before work starts.

With a staffing firm's dedicated developer, check what the contract says, because that developer is not your employee. Treat all of this as general information and ask your solicitor to check the wording.

With us, your agency owns the code, or your client does if that is your agreement with them. We transfer the repository at handover, with environment notes and an admin guide in your brand.

A note on IR35 for UK agencies

If you engage a freelancer through their own limited company, HMRC's off-payroll working rules may apply. If your agency counts as a medium or large client, you usually decide the worker's employment status. For small clients, the worker's own company decides.

A full-time freelancer who works only for your agency is the case to check most carefully. Take advice before you set one up as a dedicated developer.

Testing: ask what runs before each deploy

Laravel makes testing easy to start. Its testing documentation says Pest and PHPUnit support is included out of the box. It also says most of your tests should generally be feature tests.

Built-in support does not mean anyone wrote the tests. Ask each provider which flows have feature tests, and whether those tests run before every deploy. Better still, ask to see the output of the last test run.

We write feature tests for the flows that cost the client money if they break, such as sign-up, payment, approval and export. If you need a coverage target or your own CI setup, we put it in the scope.

Handover: the checklist to insist on

A Laravel app should change hands without a phone call to the person who built it. Ask for these items whichever model you choose.

  • The Git repository, moved to an account you or your client control
  • An up-to-date .env.example file that lists every environment variable with placeholder values
  • Secrets passed through a password manager, never committed with the code
  • Deployment notes covering queue workers, scheduled tasks and backups
  • The Laravel and PHP versions, and the dates they leave support
  • Written confirmation that the builder's access to servers and services has been removed

Laravel's own configuration docs say the .env file should not be committed to source control. If an intruder reached the repository, every credential in it would be exposed.

Check version support too. Laravel's release notes give each major release 18 months of bug fixes and two years of security fixes.

The support table on that page shows Laravel 12 stopped getting bug fixes in August 2026 and gets security fixes until February 2027. An app still on Laravel 11 or older is already outside security support.

If an inherited app needs urgent fixes first, we scope those separately from the upgrade. It is the same approach our website rescue and fixes service takes with broken client sites: find the cause, then change things.

Cost structure, without the guesswork

We will not quote market day rates here, because they vary too widely to be useful. What matters more is how each model charges and who absorbs an overrun.

  • Freelancer: you pay for time. Overruns, rework and your own review hours sit with you.
  • Dedicated developer: you pay a salary plus employer costs, or a monthly fee, in quiet months as well as busy ones.
  • White-label team: you pay a fixed price against a written scope, so the builder carries the overrun. Changes are written down and priced before anyone builds them.

We scope most Laravel applications as one-off projects with a fixed price. Where Laravel work recurs, our Premium plan from £2,400 a month covers builds alongside AI automation, SEO and paid media. It allows up to 6 active projects, and Enterprise is quoted.

A decision rule

  • Choose a freelancer when the job is small, the spec is tight and someone on your team can review PHP code.
  • Choose a dedicated developer when you have enough Laravel work to fill a full-time role every month, and someone to manage it.
  • Choose a white-label team when work arrives in projects, the client expects cover and documentation, and you want a fixed price.

Six checks before you sign anyone

  1. Who covers the work if the main developer is away for two weeks?
  2. Does the contract assign the code and the repository to us or our client?
  3. Which flows get feature tests, and do the tests run before each deploy?
  4. What does the handover pack contain, and who removes access afterwards?
  5. How are scope changes priced, and who pays for an overrun?
  6. Will you ever contact our client, or show their app in a portfolio?

A good provider answers each one in writing before the first invoice. A vague answer to the first two is the clearest warning sign.

Laravel or Next.js?

Sometimes the better question is which framework to use. Choose Laravel when the client's hosting or developers already run PHP. It also fits apps that are mostly admin screens, reports and background jobs.

If the front end is React and future developers will write TypeScript, a Next.js app on PostgreSQL may suit the client better.

Working with a white-label Laravel team

We build Laravel portals, APIs and admin panels behind your agency, on a staging URL under your brand. Our founder, Md Alamgir Hossen, has nine years of PHP work for agencies in the UK and Bangladesh. Most recently, he led the WordPress team at a UK agency.

If you want one person who knows a client's app, a monthly plan gives you a named producer with team cover behind them. Changes run through your shared channel, so nobody needs to sit inside your agency.

We sign a mutual NDA before the brief, never contact your client and fix post-launch defects inside the scope at our cost. You get a written scope with a fixed price within two business days.

Read the detail on our white-label Laravel development page. Then send us a brief for one small job, and judge the code before you commit to more.

posts.title: Figma to WordPress for Agencies: Process and Pricing
posts.excerpt: Figma to WordPress for agencies, step by step: design tokens, blocks or Elementor widgets, WCAG 2.2 checks and launch, plus what really drives the price.
posts.content_html:
Figma to WordPress for agencies works best as a fixed sequence. Turn the design's variables into tokens, map each component to a block or Elementor widget, and build templates. Then check every screen width and WCAG 2.2 before launch.

The price depends on unique templates and components far more than on page count. When we build an approved Figma file on WordPress, we send a fixed-price scope within two business days of the brief.

Here is the process step by step, what changes the price and how we scope it.

What to hand over with the Figma file

Most delays on a Figma to WordPress build start with a missing file, not with code. Before we price a build, we check the handover for these:

  • Approved frames for mobile, tablet and desktop, with the date of sign-off
  • Components with their variants and states: hover, focus, error, empty and loading
  • Variables or styles for colour, type and spacing
  • A list of templates, such as home, service, blog post, archive and contact
  • Real copy, or at least real lengths for headings and product names
  • Font licences and image rights for web use
  • Who edits the site after launch, and how often
  • Forms, CRM and tracking needs, plus a list of old URLs that will change

Client names can wait until you have the NDA. We turn anything missing into a question in the scope, so nobody prices a guess.

What we flag in the file before pricing

Some design choices cost more to build than they look. We point these out in the scope, with a cheaper option where one exists:

  • Text set inside images, which editors cannot change and screen readers cannot read
  • One-off spacing and colour values that match no token
  • Hover effects with no tap equivalent on phones
  • Fonts licensed for print but not for the web
  • Components edited by hand instead of through a variant
  • Cards that break when a heading runs long or a translation is wordier

Step 1: Turn Figma variables into design tokens

Figma stores raw values such as colours, numbers and strings as variables, grouped into collections with modes. Figma's overview of variables, collections and modes explains how aliasing one variable to another lets a team implement design tokens.

We copy those tokens into WordPress once, before we build any page:

  • Block themes: colours, font sizes and spacing become presets in theme.json. WordPress then outputs each preset as a CSS custom property, which the editor and the front end share. The WordPress theme handbook on presets explains how.
  • Elementor: tokens become global colours and global fonts. Elementor provides four default colours and four default typography sets. A custom widget control can inherit them through its global argument, as Elementor's developer docs on global styles explain.

With the tokens in place, a later brand colour change takes one edit instead of fifty.

Step 2: Map each component to a block or widget

Choose the build approach by who edits the site and how much layout freedom they need. The scope names the approach and the reason.

Figma elementCustom theme with ACFBlock themeElementor
Colour, type and spacing variablesCSS custom properties in the themetheme.json presetsGlobal colours and fonts
Repeated sections such as heroes and cardsACF field groups in fixed templatesCustom Gutenberg blocksCustom widgets in a plugin
Headers, footers and archivesTheme templatesBlock theme templatesTheme builder templates
Who it suitsEditors who fill in fixed layoutsEditors who rearrange pagesTeams who already use Elementor

Each Figma component becomes one block or widget, built once and reused. We give it the same name in code as in Figma, so your designer and our developer talk about the same thing.

Custom Elementor widgets expose only the controls the design allows, so editors change text and images while spacing and structure stay fixed. If Elementor cannot reproduce a component cleanly, the scope flags it and suggests a custom widget or a small design change.

Step 3: Build templates, then pages

We build a blog post template once, whether the site has 10 posts or 500. So we build and review each template before we fill in pages, and you sign off per template rather than per page.

We register image sizes per template and give every changed URL a tested redirect. Editor roles let the client's team publish and edit, while plugin installs and theme settings stay with an administrator.

Step 4: Check every width, not just three frames

Figma shows the frames your designer drew, usually three. A browser shows every width in between, and that is where layouts break.

We compare each built page with your frames side by side, then drag the window through the widths between them. We test on real phones and tablets as well as in desktop browsers.

WCAG 2.2 sets two checks here. Content must reflow at a width of 320 CSS pixels without scrolling in two directions. Text must also resize to 200 percent without losing content or function.

Step 5: Test accessibility against WCAG 2.2 AA

WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation on 5 October 2023. The W3C's summary of what's new in WCAG 2.2 lists nine new success criteria. Several catch problems that start in the Figma file, so we check the design first and the build again.

  • Text contrast: at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text (1.4.3).
  • Non-text contrast: at least 3:1 for input borders, icons and other parts of the interface people need to see (1.4.11).
  • Visible focus: keyboard users can always see where they are (2.4.7). Sticky headers and cookie banners must not hide the focused item completely (2.4.11, new in 2.2).
  • Target size: tap targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing around smaller ones (2.5.8, new in 2.2).
  • Dragging: sliders and drag-to-reorder lists also work with a single tap or click (2.5.7, new in 2.2).
  • Forms: every field gets a label, and multi-step forms do not ask for the same information twice (3.3.7, new in 2.2).
  • Structure: headings, lists and tables use real markup, so screen readers get the structure sighted visitors see (1.3.1).

Automated tools catch some of these. Focus order, reflow and target spacing need a person with a keyboard and a phone.

Step 6: QA, staging and launch

The build lives on a password-protected, noindexed staging site under your brand from the first day. A named producer posts progress in your shared Slack Connect or WhatsApp channel.

Before you see it, the build passes our published QA checklist: cross-browser, real-device, accessibility and Core Web Vitals checks. At launch we test redirects, forms and tracking that waits for cookie consent, then hand over an editing guide in your brand. We remove the staging site within 14 days of launch unless you ask us to keep it.

Figma to WordPress for agencies: what drives the price

Page count is a weak guide to price. A 40-page site built from five templates can cost less than a 12-page site where every page is unique. These factors move the price most:

  • the number of unique templates
  • the number of components and states to build
  • the editing approach: ACF fields, custom blocks or custom Elementor widgets
  • forms, CRM and other third-party integrations
  • how much content we migrate or enter
  • store logic, such as subscriptions, bundles or custom shipping
  • a deadline shorter than the normal turnaround

We bill premium plugins and Elementor Pro licences at cost, or you hold them in your own account. Either way, we add no mark-up.

How we scope a Figma to WordPress project

  1. You share the Figma file, the prototype and the brand system.
  2. We ask the missing questions on a short scoping call.
  3. Within two business days, you get a written scope: platform, component list, timeline and a fixed price.
  4. Nothing starts until you approve it, and we price any change in writing before anyone builds it.
  5. You sign off each template, and we fix post-launch defects in the agreed scope at our cost.

Builds can also run inside a monthly plan. Essential, from £500 a month, covers WordPress and WooCommerce builds of up to 5 pages per project. Growth (from £1,200) and Premium (from £2,400) raise the limit to 10 and 15 pages and run more projects at once.

Send us the Figma file

If you have an approved design, our white-label WordPress development team builds it with ACF templates or custom blocks. Our white-label Elementor development team builds it with custom widgets and global styles instead.

If you only have a brief, our white-label web design team produces the Figma file first, and the same team builds it. Send us the Figma link with the date you promised your client. You get a written scope and a fixed price within two business days.

posts.title: n8n Workflows for Marketing Agencies: 10 Ideas
posts.excerpt: n8n for agencies: ten practical marketing workflows with trigger, steps and result, plus what n8n's licence allows when you build for clients.
posts.content_html:
The n8n workflows that pay off fastest for an agency move leads, report data and alerts between tools clients already use. Below are ten we would build first, each with its trigger, steps and result.

We also cover what n8n for agencies means under its licence, and what it costs to run. Building workflows for clients comes with rules. Most of the ideas need no AI at all.

Ten n8n workflows for marketing agencies

Each row is one workflow. Where an AI step appears, a person checks its output before a customer sees it.

WorkflowTriggerStepsResult
1. Form leads into the CRMA webhook from the website formCheck required fields and the email format. Search the CRM by email. Create or update the contact, assign an owner and post to the sales channel.One CRM record per person, with an owner within minutes
2. Meta lead ads to salesA new lead from a Meta lead formMap form fields to CRM fields. Add the campaign and form name as the source. Alert the client's sales inbox.Paid leads reach sales while the person still remembers the ad
3. Enquiry sorting with AIA new enquiry from a form or a shared inboxAn AI step tags it (sales, support, job application or spam). Unclear items go to a person. Each tag routes to its own place.Sales sees sales enquiries, and spam never reaches the CRM
4. First reply with approvalA sales enquiry tagged by workflow 3A model drafts a reply from the client's approved FAQ. The account owner approves it in Slack. The reply goes out from the client's mailbox.Faster first replies, and nothing leaves without sign-off
5. Monthly report data pullA schedule: early on the first working day of the monthFetch last month's figures from GA4, the ad platforms and the CRM. Write them to the report sheet. Notify the account manager.Figures are ready before anyone opens the report
6. Daily lead-flow checkA schedule: every morningCount yesterday's leads per client in the CRM. Compare with the usual range. Alert if the count is zero or far below normal.A broken form or tag gets noticed in a day, not at month end
7. Closed deals back to ad platformsA deal marked qualified or won in the CRMLook up the click ID saved with the lead. Check consent. Send the outcome to the ad platform's conversion API.Bidding learns from real sales, not form fills
8. Client onboarding packA signed proposal or a submitted onboarding formCopy the folder template. Create the project and task list. Open the client channel and request access to each account you need.Every new client starts with the same checklist
9. Review requestsA job marked complete or an order fulfilledWait a set number of days. Check for an open complaint. Send the review request and log it on the contact.A steady flow of reviews without anyone remembering to ask
10. Contract renewal alertsA schedule: every MondayRead contract end dates from a sheet. Find those ending in the next 60 days. Send each account manager the client's latest figures.Renewal talks start early, with numbers to hand

Notes on the workflows that need most care

These notes cover the workflows where a mistake reaches a customer or an ad account. Here is what we check on each.

Lead workflows

Search the CRM by email before you create anything. A webhook sent twice should update one contact, not create two.

Keep the AI step in workflow 3 narrow. It picks one tag from a fixed list. Anything it is unsure about goes to a person instead of a best guess.

Worked example: workflow 1, step by step

  1. A webhook trigger receives the form post from the client's site.
  2. A check stops the run if the email is missing or malformed, and alerts the owner with the raw data attached.
  3. A CRM search looks for an existing contact with that email.
  4. The workflow creates the contact if none exists, or updates it if one does, and records the lead source.
  5. A round-robin rule picks an owner from the sales team list.
  6. A Slack message tells that owner about the lead, with a link to the CRM record.

Keep the form's own email notification running as a backup for the first few weeks. If the CRM goes down, nobody loses a lead while the alert gets fixed.

The approval step

n8n's Slack node has a Send and Wait for Response operation. It sends a message and waits for the recipient to respond before the workflow continues. Approvers can answer inside Slack, so the account owner signs off a draft without opening n8n.

Use the client's own mailbox for the final send. The reply then comes from their address, and your agency's tools stay out of sight.

Reporting and tracking

Let code do the maths in workflow 5, and keep any AI commentary as a draft for the account manager to edit. Where no built-in node covers a report you need, the HTTP Request node can call the platform's API directly.

Workflow 7 depends on consent and on saving click IDs when the form is submitted. We scope it alongside analytics and conversion tracking, because a workflow cannot send what the site never captured.

Make every workflow safe to hand over

A workflow that fails quietly is worse than none, because everyone assumes the leads still arrive. We add these to every build before handover.

  • An error workflow. The Error Trigger node starts a separate workflow when a linked workflow fails. It passes on details such as the workflow name, the error message and the last node that ran. Send those to a named person in Slack or by email.
  • Retries and batching. n8n's HTTP Request troubleshooting page describes Retry on Fail, with a maximum number of tries and a wait between them. It also describes Batching, which spaces requests out to stay inside a rate limit.
  • Duplicate protection. Check for an existing record before you write one, so a repeated webhook does no harm.
  • A runbook. One short document per workflow: what triggers it, what it touches, who gets alerts and what to check first.

One quirk from the Error Trigger docs catches people out. You cannot test an error workflow by running it by hand. It only runs when an automatic execution fails, so plan a deliberate failure in testing.

Licensing: what n8n for agencies allows

n8n's self-hosted Community edition runs under its Sustainable Use License. n8n's licence FAQ says you may build, run and maintain workflows on your own instance for clients. The condition is that clients do not access that instance directly.

The same FAQ says you can charge clients for workflow creation, setup and maintenance. You can also consult on n8n installed on a client's own server, provided you do not offer hosting as well.

Two things are not allowed under that licence. You cannot host n8n as a service where clients build their own workflows. Nor can you white-label n8n by removing its branding and offering it as is.

Delivering workflows under your agency's name is a different thing from white-labelling the n8n product. If your offer comes close to either line, ask n8n before you sell it.

Cloud or self-hosted, and what it costs

n8n's guide to choosing how to use n8n lists two routes: n8n Cloud, which n8n manages, and self-hosting on your own infrastructure. The self-hosted Community edition is free, and the Business and Enterprise editions are paid.

Self-hosting still takes work. The same guide says technical expertise is required for installation and configuration, and that you provide and manage the infrastructure.

As listed on n8n's pricing page in October 2026, both entry plans are hosted by n8n. Starter costs €20 a month, billed annually, for 2,500 workflow executions a month. Pro costs €50 a month, billed annually, for 10,000.

The same page says every plan includes unlimited users and workflows. It counts an execution as a single run of a whole workflow, however many steps it has. A lead workflow runs once per lead, so a client's monthly lead volume gives you a fair first estimate.

How we choose for a client

We prefer to build inside the client's own n8n account, so the client keeps the workflows and the bill. Self-hosting suits clients whose data should stay on infrastructure they control, as long as someone patches, monitors and backs up the server.

If the client already runs flows in Make or another tool, say so in the brief. Sometimes fixing what exists beats a rebuild.

Getting these workflows built under your brand

Pick the two or three workflows from the table that would save your team the most hours, and start there. A few reliable workflows beat twenty fragile ones.

We build n8n, Make and custom code automation white-label, with a written fixed-price scope within two business days of the brief. Our workflow automation page explains how we build, and our AI automation page covers workflows with an AI step.

We sign a mutual NDA first, never contact your client and fix post-launch defects inside the agreed scope at our cost. Send us the brief with the tools involved and rough monthly volumes.

posts.excerpt: A white label technical SEO checklist for agencies: crawl, indexing, canonicals, sitemaps, Core Web Vitals, schema and redirects, with Google's rules.
posts.content_html:
A white label technical SEO checklist lets your strategists find the problems while a partner's developers fix them under your agency's name. This one covers crawl, indexing, canonicals, sitemaps, Core Web Vitals, structured data and redirects.

Where Google publishes a rule, the item links to it. That way each fix rests on Google's own documentation, which helps when a client asks why.

How to run a white label technical SEO checklist

Split the work by who does it best. Your team runs the crawl and sets priorities. The partner fixes each item in the CMS or codebase, verifies it and logs it.

For each item, record the check, the rule, the fix and the proof in the ticket. The proof is what goes into the client report.

The checklist at a glance

AreaWhat to checkPasses when
Crawlrobots.txt, status codes and internal linksImportant pages can be crawled, and no internal link points at an error
Indexingnoindex tags and headersOnly pages you want out of Google carry noindex, and none of them is blocked in robots.txt

SitemapsXML sitemap contents and sizeOnly canonical, indexable URLs, with no file over 50,000 URLs or 50MB
Core Web VitalsField data in Search ConsoleLCP 2.5 seconds or less, INP 200 milliseconds or less, CLS 0.1 or less
Structured dataJSON-LD on key templatesValid in the Rich Results Test and true to what the page shows
RedirectsOld URLs and redirect chainsPermanent server-side redirects go straight to the final URL

1. Crawl

Start with a full crawl of the live site in Screaming Frog or a similar crawler. Then compare the crawl with the XML sitemap.

Sitemap pages that the crawl never reaches are often orphaned, with no internal links. Crawled pages missing from the sitemap may not belong in the index at all.

  • Check robots.txt for rules that block important sections, a common leftover from staging.
  • Look for filters and faceted navigation that create thousands of near-duplicate URLs.
  • List every 4xx and 5xx response, plus the internal links that point at them.
  • Check content that only appears after JavaScript runs, because a crawler may see a thin page.

Keep one rule in mind: robots.txt controls crawling, and it does not reliably keep a page out of Google. The indexing step explains why.

2. Indexing

To keep a page out of Google, use noindex, set as a robots meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header. Google's page on blocking indexing with noindex sets two rules that audits often find broken.

  • The page must not be blocked in robots.txt. If Googlebot cannot crawl it, Googlebot never sees the noindex, and the URL can still appear in results when other pages link to it.
  • Google does not support a noindex rule inside robots.txt itself.

Then check the opposite problem: pages that should rank but carry noindex. A staging setting that survived launch is the usual culprit. Check the CMS's site-wide indexing setting and the SEO plugin's rules for each template.

After a fix, Googlebot has to recrawl the page to see the change. Google notes this can take months for less important pages, and the URL Inspection tool can request a recrawl.

3. Canonicals

A canonical tells Google which URL you prefer when several URLs show the same content. Google's guide to specifying a canonical URL ranks the signals. Redirects and the canonical link tag are strong signals, while sitemap inclusion is a weak one.

  • Use absolute URLs in the canonical tag, not relative paths.
  • Link internally to the canonical URL, not to a duplicate.
  • Do not use robots.txt to choose a canonical.
  • Do not use noindex to stop Google picking a page as canonical within one site.

Typical faults include canonicals that point at a staging domain or at the wrong URL version, such as http instead of https. A crawl that compares each page's canonical with its own URL catches both.

4. XML sitemaps

A sitemap tells Google which URLs you want in search results. Google's guide to building and submitting a sitemap sets firm limits and a few rules that agencies often miss.

  • One sitemap can hold up to 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed. Split anything larger into several files.
  • Use fully qualified, absolute URLs.
  • Include the URLs you want to see in search results. In practice, leave out redirects, noindexed pages and errors.
  • Google ignores the priority and changefreq values, so do not spend time tuning them.
  • Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently accurate. It should change with a significant update, not with a new copyright year.
  • Submit the sitemap in Search Console, or add a Sitemap line to robots.txt.

On headless and Next.js builds, generate the sitemap from the real routes. A hand-maintained sitemap drifts away from the site as pages change.

5. Core Web Vitals

Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness and visual stability for real visitors. The Search Console Core Web Vitals report uses these thresholds.

MetricGoodNeeds improvementPoor
LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)2.5 seconds or less4 seconds or lessOver 4 seconds
INP (Interaction to Next Paint)200 milliseconds or less500 milliseconds or lessOver 500 milliseconds
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)0.1 or less0.25 or lessOver 0.25

The report uses real-user data from the Chrome UX Report, covering the last 28 days. Each group of similar URLs takes the status of its worst metric, measured at the 75th percentile of visits.

Once you start validation on an issue, Search Console watches for 28 days before it marks the issue fixed. Tell the client that up front, so nobody expects a green report the day after release.

Typical fixes include image size and loading priority, render-blocking CSS and fonts, heavy JavaScript, third-party scripts and reserved space for banners and embeds. A lab test in PageSpeed Insights confirms a fix on release day. Field data in Search Console is the proof the client will check.

A few template fixes fit inside technical SEO work. A slow site that needs caching, image and script work runs better as a separate Core Web Vitals optimisation project. That project reports before and after field data.

6. Structured data

Structured data describes the page to Google in a standard format. Google's general structured data guidelines recommend JSON-LD and set these rules.

  • Mark up only content that visitors can see on the page.
  • Make the markup a true representation of the page content.
  • Test it with the Rich Results Test and the URL Inspection tool.

Set the client's expectations as well. Google does not guarantee that valid markup will appear as a rich result.

A structured data manual action removes a page's eligibility for rich results, though Google says it does not affect ranking.

On WordPress, schema can come from several plugins at once. Pick one source per template, and validate it again after plugin updates.

7. Redirects

Redirects pass what an old URL earned on to its new address. Google's guide to site moves with URL changes sets the rules a migration checklist needs.

  • Use permanent server-side redirects, such as 301 or 308, from each old URL to its mapped new URL.
  • Redirect straight to the final destination. If a chain is unavoidable, Google suggests ideally no more than 3 redirects and fewer than 5.
  • Keep redirects in place for at least a year, and consider keeping them indefinitely.
  • Update internal links to the new URLs, and submit the new sitemap in Search Console.

Google also says to expect temporary ranking fluctuation during a move. Tell the client before launch, not after.

Redesigns often leave redirect problems behind, such as merged pages with no redirect or old redirects that now chain into new ones. Our website migration service builds the redirect map from a full crawl, the sitemaps, Search Console and backlink data before launch.

Handing the checklist to a white label partner

Send the audit or ticket list with priorities, and give access to the client's platform. We ask for the least access that does the job, such as a scoped CMS role and Search Console access. Hosting or repository access comes only when a fix needs it.

Each fix goes to staging first where the platform allows it. We verify it with the tools your team uses: Screaming Frog, Search Console, PageSpeed Insights and schema validators. Then we release it and log it.

The same finding needs a different fix on each platform. On WordPress, a canonical fault may sit in a theme or plugin setting. On a headless Next.js site, it lives in the metadata code.

That is why your partner needs developers on the team as well as SEO specialists.
